notes:
I found sources for most of Job 31, but some verses have little or nothing. The tool limits ran out before I could read anything on verses 16–23, 29, 31 or 39, and I got only one sentence on v. 24. The Matthew Henry full-chapter page loaded only its menu. I found nothing on the Orthodox sites or on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching for this chapter.

## The chapter as a whole
- Guzik quotes Andersen: the chapter is an "oath of clearance in the form of a negative confession," a known legal practice of the time. Guzik also quotes Mason calling it "Job's Sermon on the Mount." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-31/
- JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown): chapter 29 defended Job's public life as a leader; this chapter defends his private life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/job-31.html

## Verse notes

**v. 1**
- Traditional reading: Ellicott says Job is denying sins that others can't easily see, the hidden ones of the heart: lust and idolatry. https://biblehub.com/job/31-1.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary reads "a covenant *for* my eyes." The covenant was with himself, probably made in his youth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-1.htm
- JFB says the Hebrew wording shows the eyes were not the other party to the covenant. It was made with his own soul and with God, concerning his eyes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/job-31.html
- Bullinger (quoted by Guzik) also says the covenant was with God, against his eyes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-31/
- Hartley: in the Old Testament the eyes were the gateway to the heart (Gen 3:6; 2 Sam 11:2). The KJV Bible Commentary adds that the verb means a lingering gaze, not a brief glance. https://www.preceptaustin.org/job_311_commentary
- A different reading: Constable says "virgin" (betulah) refers to idolatry, meaning worship of "the maiden," a fertility goddess. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/31-1.html Clarke likewise thinks "Bethulah" may be an idol. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/31-1.html
- How to apply it: a Precept Austin editor's note on John Armstrong says such a covenant must be kept in the Spirit's strength. Made in our own strength, it puts us back under the law. https://www.preceptaustin.org/job_311_commentary

**vv. 2–3**
- Guzik: a woman who was not his wife was not "the allotment of God" for Job. He also says Job considered how destructive lust is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-31/

**v. 4**
- Gill gives two readings. Either Job is calling on God as witness, since God sees his ways, or he is saying that an all-seeing God would have punished him if he were guilty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-31.html
- Guzik: Job was helped by remembering that God's eye was always on him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-31/

**vv. 5–6**
- Guzik quotes Andersen: the curse of crop failure in v. 8 suggests v. 5 is about dishonest business dealing. Job was willing to be weighed on honest scales. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-31/
- Gill notes that some (following Sephorno) read v. 6 as a plain statement: "God knows my integrity." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-31.html

**v. 7**
- Gill and JFB say a heart that "followed my eyes" means greed, not lust. They compare Achan, who saw, coveted, took and hid (Josh 7:21), and "the lust of the eyes" (1 John 2:16). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-31.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/job-31.html

**v. 8**
- Gill (KJV "offspring") notes that Job's children were already dead. Some therefore think Job first swore this oath while he was still prosperous. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-31.html

**vv. 9–10**
- Gill: the heart is led astray by looking at another man's wife, not necessarily through anything she does. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-31.html
- Guzik, quoting Poole: being tempted does not excuse sin. "Grind for another" means his wife becoming another man's slave (Clarke) or his partner (Trapp). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-31/

**vv. 11–12**
- An older outline (on the Bible Hub page) says adultery should be punished by the authorities (v. 11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-1.htm
- Trapp (quoted by Guzik): Job weighed both the human punishment (v. 11) and God's punishment (v. 12). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-31/

**vv. 13–15**
- Ellicott: Job is answering Eliphaz's charge (22:8) that he oppressed the weak. He treated his servants as brothers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-31.html
- Matthew Henry: Job looked to God as both his own Judge and his servants' Maker. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/31-15.html
- Barnes said that if people believed the servant and master shared one Creator, slavery could not last. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/job/31-15.html
- Guzik: such an ethic was rare when servants were widely seen as less than human. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-31/
- Modern application: John Piper (Baptist) says Job bases his servants' rights on God's work of forming persons in the womb. He draws an argument against abortion from this. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/god-at-work-in-every-womb Jared Wilson (The Gospel Coalition) makes the same argument. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/what-does-job-3113-15-tell-us-about-the-unborn-2/

**vv. 24–25**
- JFB: greed is hidden idolatry (Col 3:5), and in vv. 26–27 Job moves on to open idolatry. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_031.cfm

**vv. 26–28**
- These verses are about worshipping the sun and moon. The NET Bible notes say the gesture of "throwing a kiss" is mentioned only here in the Old Testament, though it is known from outside the Bible. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Job+31:26,27
- JFB: the word "adoration" literally describes this gesture of kissing the hand. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_031.cfm
- Ellicott thinks it notable that Job rejects only sun and moon worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-26.htm
- Gill mentions, and rejects, Schultens's reading: flattering the powerful, "worshipping the rising sun." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/job/31-26.html
- Matthew Henry: idolatry begins in the heart and is in effect atheism, since it denies "God on high." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_031.cfm

**vv. 30, 32**
- Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: Job bore no malice toward his worst enemy and was never unkind to strangers. Hospitality is a Christian duty (1 Pet 4:9). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-26.htm

**v. 33: the clearest split between traditions**
The question is whether "like Adam" refers to Adam in the garden or simply means "as people do."
- Methodist: Wesley and Benson both say "as Adam did in Paradise." Clarke calls it "a most evident allusion to the fall." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/31-33.html
- Lutheran: Keil & Delitzsch (Delitzsch was a Lutheran scholar) reject "as men" as too weak a sense and read "like Adam." Luther's own translation, however, rendered it "as a man." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-33.htm
- Baptist: Gill allows both readings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/31-33.html
- Pulpit Commentary: doubts Job knew the Eden story and prefers "after the manner of men." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-33.htm
- Barnes: either reading fits the Hebrew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-33.htm
- Reformed: the Geneva Study Bible says Job justified himself before men, not before God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-33.htm
- Catholic: Haydock says the Hebrew has "Adam," who blamed Eve, though the name often just means "man." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/31-33.html

**v. 34**
- JFB reads this verse as the curse Job calls down: let him be put to shame before the crowd if he hid his sin from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/31-34.html

**v. 35: was Job's challenge sinful?**
- Several call it blameworthy. Gill: "a bold expression," and one of the speeches Job later repented of. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-35.htm Guzik connects it to Job's repentance in 42:5–6, and adds that Satan, not God, was the real accuser. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-31/ Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary says Job "was mistaken" (40:4–5; 1 John 1:8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-33.htm
- Barnes disagrees: "There is no irreverence" here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-35.htm
- "Signature" translates *tav*, the letter T. The Cambridge Bible says it doesn't follow that the signature was shaped like a cross. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-35.htm

**v. 37**
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: Job would approach God boldly, like a prince, instead of hiding like Adam. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/31-33.html

**vv. 38–40**
- Ellicott thinks vv. 35–37 logically belong after vv. 38–40. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/31-35.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary hears an echo of the curse on the ground for Adam and for Cain. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/31-33.html
- Gaebelein: Job even calls the land as a witness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/job-31.html
